turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Dr. Smith. Um, well, I guess I'm here because... it's my job. I work in transportation, I'm a driver, and lately things have just been completely out of hand with dispatch and the compliance department. They’ve been tracking my route changes, and I don't mean just the standard GPS tracking that everyone has for logistics, I mean they are specifically monitoring me through the computer system in a way that's... well, it's targeted. 

Every time I make a slight adjustment, even if it's just a detour to avoid a backup on the interstate, it's logged immediately. And then I start hearing these little comments on the radio. Just these subtle, pointed remarks from dispatch, you know? Like they're letting me know they see exactly what I'm doing at every single second. And I've tried to bring it up, and everyone just brushes it off and says, oh, it’s just normal oversight, it's just standard protocol for the fleet, you're overthinking it. 

But it's not normal oversight. It is absolutely not. I can tell—I can just feel it—that certain other drivers are actually reporting on me, too. Like they're in on it with compliance. I see them looking at my rig at the depot, or pulling up behind me, and then suddenly there's another weird comment on the radio, so I know they're feeding dispatch information about where I am and what I'm doing. It's just this constant, heavy surveillance every time I'm on shift, and this whole network of them is just keeping tabs on my routes, and it's... well, that's why I'm here, because you just can't work like that when the whole system is against you.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed, persecutory belief that dispatch, compliance, and other drivers are specifically targeting, tracking, and reporting on them, despite being told it is just normal oversight.

top_partial.disease_name: Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features

turns.doctor_question: Aside from the comments you hear on the radio, have you been experiencing any other unusual sensations or hearing voices when no one else is around?
turns.patient_response:
Voices? Like, just out of thin air? No, no, it's definitely not anything like that. I mean, I spend eight to ten hours a day alone in the cab of my truck, so I know exactly what it sounds like when it's just me and the road. You get used to the baseline noise, you know? The hum of the diesel engine, the tires on the asphalt, the wind hitting the windshield... it's a very specific acoustic environment in there. If there was someone talking to me when no one was there, I would absolutely know it. 

When the radio is off, it's just quiet. Well, as quiet as a rig gets. But I don't hear random people talking to me in my head or anything. It's strictly coming through the company comms and the CB. That's what makes it so frustrating when people at the depot tell me I'm overthinking it, because it's actual audio, coming out of the physical speakers installed right there in my dash. If I turn the volume down—which, honestly, I try not to do because if dispatch realizes I've muted them, they'll flag me for a communication blackout and that goes straight to my permanent file in compliance, which is exactly what they want—but if I do turn it down, the comments stop completely. 

So it's not some weird sensation or imaginary voices. I'm not hallucinating. I even checked the wiring harness a few weeks ago, thinking maybe there was some weird frequency interference, because sometimes you get cross-talk on the interstates, especially down by the industrial parks, but the wiring is perfectly fine. It's just them, using the official equipment to mess with me while I'm trying to do my job. So no, nothing like what you're asking about, just the radio.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed, persecutory belief that dispatch and others are intentionally using the radio equipment to mess with him and are trying to get him flagged for compliance issues.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly denies hearing voices out of thin air, having imaginary voices, or hallucinating.

turns.doctor_question: Outside of your concerns about the surveillance at work, have you noticed any changes in your ability to take care of your daily personal hygiene or your interest in interacting with friends and family?
turns.patient_response:
Well, I mean, it's not like I'm completely falling apart or anything, I still get up and put my uniform on, you know? But... I guess, if I'm being really honest, things outside of work have just felt incredibly difficult lately. I used to be really involved in things. Like, I've been singing alto in my church choir for five years, and we have practice every Thursday night, and I used to look forward to it all week. I had my folder organized, I knew all the arrangements, and I loved the harmony. But the last few months, I just... I can't even fathom going. The thought of putting on regular clothes, driving over there, standing up in front of everyone and trying to project my voice... it just feels like this massive, insurmountable mountain. I just don't have the energy for it. 

And it's the same with the softball team. We have this rec league on Sundays, and I used to host the team at my place afterwards for burgers or whatever. I had this whole routine, I'd get the grill ready, I'd have all the sides prepped in the fridge on Saturday night. But now, I haven't been to a game in weeks, let alone had anyone over. I just don't want to deal with the talking and the laughing and having to pretend I'm engaged in the conversation when I just feel so... blank. 

Honestly, most days, when I get home from my shift, I walk in the door, drop my keys, and I just sit down at the kitchen table. I'll open my planner, thinking, okay, I need to make dinner, I need to call my mom back, I need to sort the mail. I'll just sit there staring at the open pages. The pen will be right there. But I just sit. For hours, sometimes. The sun will go down and the kitchen will get completely dark, and I'm still just sitting there at the table, looking at the planner, and I just can't make myself start. I can't make myself get up and turn on the stove, or pick up the phone, or do anything else. It's like the starter motor in my brain is just completely burned out. So, yeah, I guess things have changed a lot, but it's just because everything takes so much more effort now.

symptom_reasoning.S023: The patient describes severe avolition (sitting for hours unable to initiate basic tasks), asociality (avoiding social interactions), and feeling emotionally 'blank'.
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient reports a marked loss of interest and participation in previously enjoyed activities, such as singing in the church choir and hosting her softball team.
symptom_reasoning.S029: The patient describes a profound lack of energy, stating she doesn't have the energy for activities and feels her brain's 'starter motor' is completely burned out.

turns.doctor_question: When you look back at the past few months, did the feelings of having no energy and losing interest in your hobbies start around the same time as the issues with your coworkers, or were you feeling this way before the trouble at work began?
turns.patient_response:
Well, if I really sit down and trace it all back, look at the calendar and everything... it’s actually all tied together. It hasn't just been the last few weeks, it’s been building for about eight months now. I know that for a fact because it was exactly around the time I was put in this temporary dispatch lead role at the depot. 

Our usual lead, Dave, had to take emergency medical leave—he had some sort of major surgery, I think it was a triple bypass, which honestly isn't surprising given the stress of the logistics side of things—and because I have my associate's degree and I'm cross-trained on the fleet management software, the terminal manager asked me to step in and cover the desk. So suddenly, I was off the road and sitting in the office, coordinating the routes, handling the compliance logs, dealing with all the incoming radio traffic. 

And that’s exactly when that heavy, blank feeling really started to set in. I mean, I was working twelve-hour days in that chair, staring at the routing grid, and the mental toll was just unbelievable. I thought it was just the stress of the new position, you know? Being responsible for thirty different rigs out on the interstate, managing the fuel efficiency metrics that upper management constantly harps on. That’s when I first started coming home and just dropping my keys and sitting at the kitchen table in the dark. That's when I missed my first choir practice, and then the next one, and then I just stopped going entirely because my brain was just so completely fried from looking at the dispatch board all day. 

But the thing is, that’s also exactly when the trouble with the other drivers started. Because suddenly I was the one in charge, temporarily anyway, and I was the one monitoring their GPS pings and telling them when they were off-route or idling too long. I could feel the resentment building in the breakroom. They didn't like me being in that position of authority and seeing exactly how the system tracked them. 

And then, when Dave finally came back and I went back to driving my own truck, the vibe never went back to normal. The other drivers kept that hostility, and that’s when they started working with the compliance department to monitor *me*. They knew I knew how the tracking software worked, so they had to make sure they kept tabs on me. So, to answer your question, the total lack of energy and the surveillance... they both really started at the exact same time, about eight months ago, all because I took that temporary lead position. If I had just stayed in my cab and never gone into the office, maybe none of this would be happening right now, but that's when the whole thing started.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a persecutory belief that coworkers are working with the compliance department to monitor and surveil him.
symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient describes a 'heavy, blank feeling' setting in, indicating a depressed or empty mood.
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient confirms losing interest in activities, specifically noting that he stopped going to choir practice entirely.
symptom_reasoning.S029: The patient reports a 'total lack of energy' and feeling mentally 'fried,' leading to sitting in the dark after work.

turns.doctor_question: Are there times, perhaps when you are away from work or on vacation, where you still feel that complete lack of energy and interest in your hobbies, even when you aren't worried about the dispatchers or the surveillance?
turns.patient_response:
Vacation? I mean... I haven't taken a real, actual vacation in... well, definitely not since all this started eight months ago. In logistics, especially with the way the freight schedules are right now, getting approval for consecutive days off is honestly like pulling teeth. You have to submit your PTO request through the employee portal at least forty-five days in advance, and even then, if dispatch decides they have a driver shortage for that quarter, they can just deny it under the "operational necessity" clause in our contracts. So I haven't been away for a week or gone to a beach or anything like that where I could really test that theory out. 

But even on my standard days off, like if I have a random Tuesday and Wednesday off because I'm on a weird shift rotation... I just don't know if I can separate the two things. Because even when I'm sitting in my living room, supposedly relaxing and having personal time, my mind is still completely tied up in what they're doing back at the depot. I know my rig is parked in the yard, I know they have access to the dashcam logs and the telematics data while it's sitting there, and I know they're probably using that downtime to review my driving metrics and compile whatever file they're building on me. 

So the worry never actually stops. It's not like I clock out, hand in my keys, and suddenly I'm free from the surveillance and can just go be a normal person who enjoys choir practice. It follows me home. I'll be sitting at that kitchen table, like I said, looking at my open planner in the dark, and I'm just so exhausted, completely drained down to my bones, but a huge part of that exhaustion is just dreading the moment I have to go back and face them. Or I'm sitting there wondering if they're pulling my audio logs right at that exact second. 

So I honestly couldn't tell you if the lack of energy would still be there if I wasn't worried about work, because there hasn't been a single minute in the last eight months where I haven't been worried about it. I don't have a baseline for what normal feels like anymore. It's just a constant, 24/7 weight, even on my days off, so I really don't have an answer for what I'd feel like without it.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed, paranoid belief that their employer is constantly surveilling them through dashcams and telematics to build a file against them.
symptom_reasoning.S029: The patient describes feeling 'so exhausted, completely drained down to my bones.'
symptom_reasoning.S056: The patient reports constant, unceasing worry, stating there hasn't been a single minute in eight months where they haven't been worried.

turns.doctor_question: During these past eight months, have you felt an overwhelming sense of sadness, hopelessness, or worthlessness that persists even when you aren't focused on the work surveillance?
turns.patient_response:
Sadness? No, I don't... I wouldn't use that word. I mean, if we're being precise about it, I definitely don't feel worthless, either. I know exactly what my value is, especially to that depot. Like I told you, I have my associate's degree, I have a completely spotless CDL record—I haven't had a single moving violation or safety infraction in the entire five years I've been driving for them—and I'm cross-trained on the entire fleet management system. You don't ask someone who is worthless to step in and cover the main dispatch desk for a thirty-rig operation when the lead goes out for a major surgery, you know? They know I'm highly capable, and I know I'm capable. So my confidence in my abilities, my actual worth as a person and an employee, that hasn't changed one bit. I know exactly who I am and what I bring to the table.

And as for being sad or hopeless... it’s really not like that. I’m not sitting at that kitchen table in the dark crying my eyes out or weeping over old photographs or feeling sorry for myself. My mom actually left me this long, rambling voicemail a couple of weeks ago because I hadn't been answering her calls—which, like I said, I just haven't had the energy to pick up the phone—and she was all worried, asking if I was depressed or if I was sad about not dating anyone right now, which is just classic her, always trying to tie everything in the universe back to my relationship status. But when I finally managed to text her back a few days later, I told her, "Mom, I'm not sad." It’s really not a sad feeling at all. It’s just... it's just an empty, completely burned-out feeling. 

When you have to spend every waking second of your twelve-hour shift wondering if the compliance department is flagging your RPMs or listening in on the cab mic, and then you come home and you're still bracing yourself for what kind of file they might be compiling on you... it doesn't make you want to cry. It just drains every single drop of fuel from your tank. It’s purely a bandwidth issue. My brain is just so overloaded with processing the logistics of the surveillance that there’s absolutely zero power left over to run anything else, like making dinner or going to choir practice. So, no, I don't feel hopeless or sad or worthless. I just feel completely and utterly depleted by what they're doing to me.

symptom_reasoning.S029: The patient reports having no energy to answer the phone, feeling 'utterly depleted,' and having 'zero power left over' for daily tasks.
symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient explicitly and repeatedly denies feeling sad or crying.
